name: The Class for Representing a TV (Case 1)
description: Construct a class that represents a TV. The class should contain data that represents the TV's state (power on or off, current channel). The state of the TV could be accessed or changed only through the getter and setter methods. The class should also include methods to change the state of the TV (turn on/off, change channels). Assume that the valid channel range is from 1 to 120 (both inclusive).

commentList: Purpose: This line declares a new class named TV1 — a blueprint that you will use to create TV objects with their own state and behavior.

Syntax and semantics: The keyword class followed by the class name and a colon starts a new indented block. Everything indented under this line becomes part of the TV1 class (its attributes and methods).
What it means at runtime: When Python executes this line it creates the class object TV1; methods are not run yet. Later you create instances with tv = TV1() to get a usable TV object.

Common errors and misconceptions: If you forget the colon or use wrong indentation you'll get a SyntaxError or IndentationError. Putting a digit first in the class name (e.g., 1TV) is invalid. If the class body were empty you must write pass to avoid an error.

Best practices: Use a clear, descriptive name in CamelCase (TV1 is okay but TV would be clearer). Do not put a space before the colon (write class TV1:). Add a short docstring under this line to explain the class purpose, and avoid names that shadow built-in identifiers.

Inheritance note (simple): You don't need to write (object) in Python 3 — class TV1: already creates a new-style class. If you do want to inherit from another class you would put the parent(s) in parentheses after the name.
Visibility hint: This line only defines the class; the private attributes (like __on) and methods you see later are defined inside the class body and control how users interact with each TV instance.

commentList: This line defines the constructor method that runs automatically when you create a TV1 object — it sets up the object's initial state so the rest of the methods can work.

Breakdown of the syntax: 'def' starts a function definition, '__init__' is the special constructor name Python looks for, '(self)' means the method receives the instance you're creating, and the trailing ':' begins the indented body that follows.

You must include 'self' as the first parameter so you can store attributes on that specific instance (for example, self.__on and self.__channel). If you forget 'self' you'll get errors when you try to use instance attributes.

Common mistakes to watch for: missing the colon or incorrect indentation produces a SyntaxError; trying to return a value from __init__ is incorrect (it should return None); and failing to initialize attributes here can make other methods fail later.

Best practices: keep __init__ focused on creating and initializing the instance attributes that other methods expect, initialize every attribute you will use, and choose your attribute naming convention (double underscore triggers name-mangling for stronger privacy, but a single underscore is often enough and simpler).

commentList: You are creating an instance attribute that records whether the TV is powered on; setting it to False makes the TV start in the OFF state.
You can read the pieces: self is the current object, __on is the attribute name (double underscore triggers name mangling), = is the assignment operator, and False is the boolean value assigned.

You should understand the effect: this line actually creates the attribute on each TV1 object and subsequent methods (turn_on, turn_off, is_on, and the channel-change guards) read or change this value to control behavior.

You might make mistakes like omitting self (which would create a local variable instead of an attribute), using lowercase false (which is a NameError), or expecting double-underscore to make the attribute truly inaccessible (it only name-mangles it; external access is still possible via _TV1__on).

For best practice, you should initialize all instance state in __init__, prefer clear boolean names (e.g., is_on) for readability, and access this attribute only through the provided getter/setter methods rather than manipulating the mangled name directly.

commentList: Purpose: This line guards the channel change so that you only set a new channel when the TV is turned on (self.__on) and the requested channel is inside the allowed range 1 to 120.

Syntax/semantics: it is an if statement that requires all three conditions to be true (self.__on and new_channel >= 1 and new_channel <= 120). The 'and' operator means Python evaluates left to right and stops early if one condition is false (short-circuit evaluation).

Common errors & misconceptions: if new_channel is not a number (for example a string) the comparisons can raise a TypeError; using 'or' instead of 'and' would let invalid inputs through; also remember this method currently silently does nothing when the check fails, which can confuse you if you expect feedback.

Best practices: consider using the chained comparison 1 <= new_channel <= 120 for readability, validate or convert the input type (or raise a ValueError) instead of failing silently, and store 1 and 120 in named constants (e.g., MIN_CHANNEL, MAX_CHANNEL) so you and others can change limits easily.

commentList: Purpose: This line makes sure the TV is turned on and the current channel is less than 120 before allowing the channel to increase. You only proceed to change the channel when both conditions are true.

Syntax and meaning: 'if' starts a conditional. 'self.__on' is the private boolean attribute that tells you whether the TV is on. 'and' requires both sides to be True (it short-circuits). 'self.__channel < 120' checks the upper channel limit. The ':' starts the block that runs when the whole condition is True.

Common mistakes and pitfalls: You might accidentally write '<= 120', which would allow the channel to become 121 after incrementing. If you forget to check 'self.__on', you could change channels while the TV is off. Also be careful about types — comparing a non-integer channel to 120 could raise a TypeError.

Best practices: Use a named constant (for example MAX_CHANNEL = 120) instead of the magic number 120 so you can change the range easily. Consider handling the else case (e.g., return a status or log a message) so you know when a channel change was ignored. Always use the class methods to enforce rules rather than accessing attributes directly.

Behavior note: Because 'and' short-circuits, if the TV is off the second check (channel < 120) won't run. This is efficient and prevents unnecessary checks, but keep it in mind if you later add expressions with side effects.

Syntax breakdown: print(...) calls the print function; "tv2's channel is " is a string literal; + concatenates strings; str(...) converts the numeric channel to a string; tv2.get_channel() calls the get_channel method on the tv2 object (the dot accesses the method and the trailing () invokes it).

Potential error / common misconception: If you omit str(...) and try to do "..." + tv2.get_channel(), Python will raise a TypeError because you cannot concatenate a str and an int. Also remember + here is string concatenation, not numeric addition.

distractors.description: You might write this because you think Python will pass the instance automatically and you only need to list the data you want to set. If you use this line, calling tv1.set_channel(30) will raise a TypeError at runtime saying the method was given 2 arguments but only expects 1. That happens because when you call an instance method Python implicitly passes the instance as the first argument; by omitting 'self' you have the wrong number of parameters. This prevents the method from running at all, so the channel will never be changed and your program will crash when you try to set a channel. The problem here is the missing explicit reference to the instance: you haven't declared a parameter that receives the TV object, so the method signature doesn't match how instance methods are called in Python.

distractors.code: if new_channel >= 1 or new_channel <= 120 and self.__on :
distractors.description: You might pick this because you think using 'or' will still check both range ends, or you expect the power check to be applied somewhere in the expression. However, due to operator precedence this is evaluated in an unexpected way: the 'and' binds tighter than 'or', so the expression behaves like (new_channel >= 1) or ((new_channel <= 120) and self.__on). That means many values (for example any channel >= 1) will satisfy the condition regardless of whether the TV is on. As a result, the program could set the channel even when the TV is off or accept clearly out-of-intended-range values without the power check being enforced. This distractor is wrong because it mixes operators so the power-state check is not reliably applied to the whole range check.

Why you might pick this: you may think that using a simpler attribute name is fine and that the rest of the class will see the change. It's tempting because it looks like an assignment that updates the channel.

What this line actually does: it creates or updates a different attribute named channel (a public attribute) on the object. The class's getter get_channel returns the private attribute with the original name, so that getter will keep returning the old value. The class methods that check or change the channel expect the private attribute, so your change will be invisible to them.

How it affects the program: the channel appears unchanged when you call get_channel or use other TV methods, even though a new attribute exists on the object. The program runs without errors, but the setter silently fails to update the TV's real state.

Why this is invalid here: the code relies on a specially named private attribute to store the TV state. By writing to a different attribute you don't update that state. The missing piece is that you're not assigning to the same attribute the rest of the class uses, so the change has no effect.
